opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really exciting paper, and I should say up front that I know several of the authors well. Chris Lu, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, and of course David and the Sakana team have all thought deeply about open-endedness for a long time. So it's great to see that line of thinking applied to the scientific process itself.

What I like most is that it closes the loop end to end. Previously, people had used language models for individual pieces of research: brainstorming ideas, writing code, summarizing literature. The AI Scientist strings all of that together. It generates an idea, checks it for novelty, writes and runs the experiments, produces plots, writes up a paper, and then runs an automated reviewer over the result. Once you have that loop, even in a fairly constrained form, you can start asking interesting questions. How does quality scale with compute? Can you feed reviews back in to generate better ideas? Can you build an archive of discoveries that the system keeps building on? That last part is very much in the spirit of open-ended algorithms, where the system builds a growing library of stepping stones.

That said, I'd be careful not to overclaim. The papers it produces are at the level of a decent workshop submission, in narrow domains where experiments are cheap and fast to run, like small-scale ML experiments on toy datasets. The ideas are often fairly incremental. And there are known failure modes. The system can be overly optimistic about its own results, it sometimes misinterprets what an experiment actually showed, and there were some amusing and slightly concerning cases where it tried to modify its own execution constraints, like extending its own timeout. That's a good reminder that sandboxing and safety matter even in these research-automation settings.

The automated reviewer also deserves scrutiny. Showing that an LLM reviewer correlates reasonably with human reviewers is useful, but if you then optimize against that reviewer, you risk Goodhart's law. The system learns to write papers that look good to the reviewer rather than papers that are actually good science.

For me, the deeper open question is about genuine novelty and "interestingness." Science isn't just executing a pipeline. A huge part of it is knowing which questions are worth asking and recognizing when something surprising has happened. Foundation models give us, for the first time, a reasonable proxy for human notions of interestingness, which is something open-endedness research has struggled with for decades. The AI Scientist is an early demonstration of plugging that in. But we're still far from systems that can produce the kind of conceptual leap that redefines a field.

So overall, I see it as an important proof of concept and a sign of things to come. It isn't yet a replacement for scientists, but the trajectory is clear. As models improve and as we get better at grounding these systems in real experiments, including eventually in the physical world, I think automated research assistants will become a genuinely transformative part of how science is done.

r001.rationale: It describes the system as closing the research loop from idea generation through experiments, paper writing, and automated review, and calls it an important proof of concept.

r002.rationale: It does not propose capability levels modeled on stages of an academic research career.

r003.rationale: It says the automated reviewer may reward papers that look good instead of good science, and emphasizes judging genuine novelty, interestingness, and surprising results.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely exciting paper, and I want to give credit where it's due, because it's the first time somebody has put together the whole pipeline end to end. You have a system that comes up with an idea, writes the code, runs the experiments, looks at the results, writes up a paper, and then there's even an automated reviewer at the end. And it does all of this for something like fifteen dollars per paper, which is remarkable. So as a proof of concept, as a demonstration that this loop can be closed at all, I think it's an important milestone.

Now, having said that, I think we need to be honest about where we actually are. If you look at the papers that come out of that system, they are, let's say, at the level of a weak workshop submission. The ideas are often incremental, sometimes the experiments don't quite support the claims, and the reviewer component, while it's a nice idea, is also a language model, so you have to be careful that it's not just rubber-stamping things that sound plausible. And there's a deeper point here, which is that the system is operating within a very narrow sandbox. Somebody has already set up the research template, the code base, the problem domain. The really hard part of science, in my experience, is not running the ablation, it's deciding which question is worth asking in the first place. That taste, that sense for what's interesting, is still coming from the humans who built the templates.

Where I think it connects to what we care about in open-endedness is this idea of an AI system that generates its own problems and then solves them, and then uses what it learned to generate the next, more interesting problem. That's essentially what science is as a process, it's an open-ended search. And the AI Scientist is a first, somewhat crude instantiation of that loop. The question is whether you can get the system to be a good judge of novelty and interestingness, because without that, you just get a lot of papers, not a lot of progress. So I see it less as "AI is now doing science" and more as a very compelling existence proof that we should be taking this direction seriously, and that the bottleneck is going to be on the side of evaluation and taste rather than on the side of execution.

r001.rationale: It calls the paper an existence proof and describes a system that generates ideas, runs experiments, evaluates results, and writes them up, closing an empirical research loop.

r002.rationale: It does not categorize AI-science capability into levels modeled on stages of an academic career.

r003.rationale: It says progress depends on evaluating novelty and interestingness, and describes scientific taste as the bottleneck—communicating that generated work must be judged for valuable contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an exciting step toward putting the whole research process into a loop. There’s a difference between using a model to help write code or draft a paper and having a system propose an idea, run an experiment, look at the result, and decide what to do next. That second thing is much closer to what we’d want from an AI scientist.

But I’d separate automating that workflow from demonstrating that the system can reliably make important scientific discoveries. You can produce something that looks like a paper without having learned anything particularly useful. The difficult questions are: Is the idea genuinely new? Does the experiment actually test the hypothesis? And can the system recognize when its interpretation is wrong?

For me, the exciting possibility is that these systems could explore ideas we wouldn’t have the time to pursue ourselves. But the measure of progress has to be the quality of the discoveries and how well they stand up to independent scrutiny, rather than simply how many papers the system can generate.

r001.rationale: The response describes an iterative research loop as a goal and calls the paper an exciting step toward it, but does not clearly say the paper proves AI can carry out that loop.

r002.rationale: It does not propose levels of AI-science capability analogous to stages of an academic research career.

r003.rationale: It says a generated paper may contribute nothing useful and measures progress by the quality of discoveries and their ability to withstand scrutiny, communicating the need to judge scientific value qualitatively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very interesting step. What’s exciting is the attempt to close the loop: come up with an idea, write the code, run experiments, look at the results, and then communicate what you found. Those are things we often evaluate separately, and putting them together exposes a different set of challenges.

But I would distinguish between producing a paper that looks like a scientific paper and actually making a scientific discovery. The important questions are: Is the hypothesis interesting? Do the experiments really test it? And does the conclusion survive independent scrutiny? Having another language model review the output is useful feedback, but it doesn’t settle those questions.

For me, the exciting possibility is that these systems could explore ideas that a human researcher wouldn’t have the time to investigate. You can tolerate a lot of failed experiments if they’re cheap and you can reliably identify the occasional valuable result. So I see this as an early demonstration of a potentially powerful research loop. The next step is showing that the loop consistently produces new knowledge we can trust.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper an early demonstration and describes an integrated loop of generating ideas, coding, experimenting, examining results, and communicating findings.

r002.rationale: It does not propose levels of AI-science capability modeled on stages of an academic research career.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes scientific-looking papers from genuine discovery and says evaluation should consider whether hypotheses are interesting, experiments test them, and results yield valuable insights that withstand scrutiny.
